title: One-at-a-Time Quantum Guessing: Multipartite Entanglement Beyond MoE Games
abstract: Multipartite entanglement remains a challenging and not fully understood aspect of quantum information. Monogamy-of-Entanglement (MoE) games have been highly effective for studying limitations on the usefulness of entanglement imposed by monogamy constraints. To better reveal the extent to which multipartite entanglement can be useful, we introduce a class of quantum guessing games, termed One-at-a-Time Guessing (OTG) games. In these games, quantum players individually guess the outcomes of random measurements performed by a referee on a pre-shared entangled state. Unlike MoE games, OTG games select players individually at random according to a specified probability distribution, thereby probing each player's correlation with the referee. We show that, despite monogamy constraints, players sharing certain entangled states can moderately outperform those relying only on classical uncertainty. This advantage arises even in simple OTG games involving only Pauli measurements on qubits, where optimal entanglement increases the winning probability by at least 4%. This contrasts with MoE games, where shared entanglement has been shown in several settings to provide only limited (if any) advantage over classical strategies. We further establish a majorization property: the value of an OTG game respects the majorization ordering of the player-selection probability distribution. We also analyze in detail a two-player OTG game in which the referee measures one of the three Pauli observables on a qubit, and show that it is optimally played using a specific parameterized family of three-qubit $W$-like states. These results suggest that OTG games provide a useful framework for investigating the usefulness of multipartite entanglement in multiparty quantum correlations.
summary: This paper introduces One-at-a-Time Quantum Guessing (OTG) games as a new tool to study multipartite entanglement beyond the limitations of standard MoE games. The authors demonstrate that in these games, shared entanglement provides a tangible advantage over classical strategies, even when constrained by entanglement monogamy. This suggests OTG games are a valuable resource for understanding the practical utility of complex quantum correlations.
main_problem: The paper aims to investigate the usefulness of multipartite entanglement in a setting that moves beyond the constraints imposed by Monogamy-of-Entanglement (MoE) games.
main_result: The introduced One-at-a-Time Guessing (OTG) games show that shared entanglement can provide a measurable advantage (at least 4% in simple qubit cases) over classical strategies, contrasting with some findings in MoE games.
method: The authors introduce and analyze OTG games, which involve individual random guessing by players on a shared entangled state, and establish mathematical properties like the majorization ordering for the game's value.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum guessing game framework involving multiple players sharing a pre-shared entangled state, where a referee performs random measurements. The analysis uses qubits and Pauli measurements, and the optimal states are shown to be related to W-like states.
key_observables: The winning probability ($\omega$) of the game, which quantifies the advantage gained by using entanglement over classical correlation.
important_parameters: The player-selection probability distribution ($p$ or $q$), which dictates which player guesses at any given time.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the framework of quantum non-local games and the use of the NPA hierarchy to bound the game's value.
paper_structure: The paper introduces OTG games as a variant of non-local games, compares them to MoE games, establishes the majorization property relating game value to player selection probabilities, and provides detailed analyses using semidefinite programming bounds.
why_interesting: It provides a novel, structured framework (OTG games) to quantify the utility of multipartite entanglement in correlation tasks, offering insights into how entanglement resources can be utilized in sequential or individual measurement settings, which is relevant for quantum communication protocols.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: A hierarchy of related quantum games. Arrows denote inclusion (e.g. measurement-result quantum guessing games are a subclass of extended non-local games). We propose the variant of one-at-a-time quantum guessing games.

Fig. 2: Pictorial representation of the two-player three Pauli-basis OTG game. A tripartite state ρABC is initally shared amongst all three participants. Alice randomly selects an Pauli observable θ ∈{X, Y, Z} and a random player i ∈{Bob, Charlie}. She measures her qubit with observable θ and obtains a measurement outcome x ∈{0, 1}. The data (θ, i) is announced to both Bob and Charlie, and the selected player i performs a measurement to obtain a measurement outcome x′ ∈{0, 1}. The game is won if x = x′.

Fig. 3: Bounds on the value ω2(G, q) of the two-player three Pauli-basis OTG game as a function of the player selection probability q = (qB, qC). The lower bound from the parametrized qubit strategy agrees well with the upper bound from the second level SDP of the NPA hierarchy, up to numerical precision. The upper bound from the first level SDP of the NPA hierarchy is notably looser when the player selection probabilities are roughly equal.
Fig. 4: Coefficients of the parameterized optimal state |ψ⟩= α |001⟩+ β |010⟩+ γ |100⟩for the two-player three Pauli-basis OTG game, as a function of the player selection probability q = (qB, qC).

Fig. 5: An illustration of various scenarios related to non-local state discrimination and hypothesis testing. Both Monogamy-of-Entanglement games and One-at-a-Time Guessing games can be viewed as examples of entanglement-mediated local hypothesis tests.
